implementation_notes: TypeScript uses the runner's spy but keeps types: jest.spyOn(object, 'method') returns a typed mock whose type is the source function (jest.Spied<typeof object.method>), so mockImplementation/mockReturnValue and expect(...).toHaveBeenCalledWith stay type-checked, while calls are tracked and the real method runs by default. What replaces the classic spy object is the runtime mock plus the compile-time Spied<Source>/mocked() mapping - the interface cannot silently drift because the compiler checks the spied member.
pitfalls: jest.spyOn mutates the shared module object; without restoreAllMocks in afterEach the wrapper leaks into later tests.
Spying on a type-only interface member compiles but has nothing to wrap at runtime - the target must be a real property of an object.
For ESM/CJS interop, named exports are read-only bindings, so spying on them often records nothing; prefer dependency injection or jest.mock for that seam.

variants.name: Vitest vi.spyOn (typed, ESM-native, resource-managed restore)
variants.implementation_notes: Vitest offers the same shape for ESM-first projects: vi.spyOn is generic over the object and member (vi.spyOn<T, K extends keyof T>(object, key)), mockImplementation/mockReturnValue keep the member's types, and restoration can be automatic - vi.restoreAllMocks() or explicit resource management with `using spy = vi.spyOn(...)`, which calls mockRestore when the block exits. What replaces the classic spy is the runner's typed spy with block-scoped lifetime.
pitfalls: vi.spyOn cannot wrap primitives or non-configurable properties, and ESM module bindings are read-only - spy on an object's method instead.
vi.restoreAllMocks does not clear mock history or reset implementations, so call-count assertions on a reused spy can see stale calls.
